name: Fast C++ CSV Parser
workload: Reading a generated 8-column CSV (id,city,state,category,amount,quantity,flag,note) of 500K or 5M rows with clean and quoted-field profiles, in a count-rows loop and a full read loop into std::string cells, warm cache, single parser worker, Google Benchmark median real time.
claimed_speedup: 500K clean: count rows 81.8 ms vs 146.5 ms (~1.8x, derived from page data), read 82.8 ms vs 164.9 ms (~2.0x, derived from page data); 500K quoted: count 118.8 ms vs 197.2 ms, read 136.2 ms vs 223.5 ms (~1.6x, derived from page data); 5M clean read 944.2 ms vs 1,087 ms (~1.15x, derived from page data). Reversed on 5M count (881.5 ms vs 547.6 ms for csv-parser), in materialization tables, and against csv-parser positional reads with 4+ parser workers.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.50 (Visual Studio 2026), C++20, CMake Release configuration (optimization flags implied by the Release config, not spelled out), AVX2 enabled, CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, Google Benchmark 1.8.5
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12400 (12 logical CPUs, ~2.5 GHz), Windows 11 Home 25H2, Samsung 990 EVO SSD
tradeoffs: Single header csv.h. Column count and types are fixed at compile time (read_header plus read_row with typed arguments), so there is no dynamic row model. Does not parse quoted fields with embedded line breaks (the comparison marks the multiline profile unsupported). Optional background I/O thread (needs pthread with GCC, or CSV_IO_NO_THREAD). The caller owns row materialization and any parallelism.
caveats: The benchmark is in the competitor's repo (csv-parser author), not the project's own, and it was written to show where csv-parser wins: fast-cpp-csv-parser loses the 5M-row count benchmark, both materialization tables and the 4+ worker positional-read comparison. Windows/MSVC only, one machine, Google Benchmark overhead included. The fast-cpp-csv-parser source is fetched from master at build time, so no commit is pinned. Optimization flags are implied by CMake Release rather than listed, so tier A is borderline. The README of fast-cpp-csv-parser itself has no numbers, and no measurement against the guessed std::getline baseline was found (dfglib's csvPerformanceRuns.md only compares it with dfglib's own readers).
found_via: seed-record pass from the awesome-cpp CSV list entry given in the task lead; benchmark found via WebSearch 'C++ CSV parser benchmark comparison fast-cpp-csv-parser csv2 lazycsv rapidcsv vincentlaucsb csv-parser results' and the csv-parser README link to benchmarks/README.md

name: Hoedown
workload: Markdown to HTML conversion of a large Markdown file in cmark's own benchmark (the cited page does not name the input; cmark's benchmarks.md of the same era used a 10-11 MB concatenation of the Pro Git sources, timed with `time`, median of ten runs).
claimed_speedup: hoedown 0.21 s vs cmark 0.29 s (~1.4x faster, derived from page data). The same page says cmark is about six times faster than discount, so hoedown is roughly 8x faster than discount (chained, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Pure C99 library with no dependencies and a separate renderer. Targets the original Markdown 1.0.x test suites, not CommonMark. Does not sanitize HTML unless HTML_ESCAPE or HTML_SKIP is set. Treats non-ASCII punctuation and whitespace as word characters.
caveats: The numbers come from the cmark authors' own comparison page (a competing project), with no hardware, flags or input file on that page (cmark's benchmarks.md of that period names an ancient Thinkpad with a 2 GHz Core 2 Duo). Same page reports hoedown taking 17.84 s on a 50000-deep nested bracket input where cmark took 0.073 s user time, and lists many parsing bugs as of hoedown v3.0.3. The README's own claim ('up to 40 times faster than other native alternatives' when wrapped in Python or Ruby) names no baseline and has no data. Repository dormant since December 2015. cmark has been optimized since, and cmark's current benchmarks.md no longer lists hoedown or sundown.
found_via: seed-record pass from the awesome-c Utilities list entry given in the task lead; benchmark found via WebSearch 'hoedown markdown parser benchmark seconds compared discount cmark sundown md4c' which surfaced cmark's why-cmark-and-not-x.md

name: flex
workload: Running generated C-language tokenizers (recognizing keywords) over a 28,088-line, 685K-character C input; run time of the scanner (snippet only).
claimed_speedup: AT&T lex 29.8 s vs flex 19.3 s with default full table compression (~1.5x, derived), 9.0 s with flex -cfe (~3.3x, derived), 7.8 s with flex -cf (~3.8x, derived); snippet also states a factor of about 3 over lex for a scanner of about the same size. Snippet only, see caveats.
compiler_and_flags: flex table options -cfe, -cf and default compression (1988 option syntax); AT&T lex; C compiler and flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; standard scanner generator shipped by Linux and BSD distributions
tradeoffs: Table-driven DFA scanners; the fastest modes (-Cf, -CF) trade large tables for speed. Matching NUL bytes is slow. Interactive scanners are slower. The -l lex-compatibility option is documented as a major performance loss. Lexer only, no Unicode-aware matching.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: the lex vs flex timings were read from WebSearch result text attributed to a 1988 comp.compilers posting (compilers.iecc.com articles such as 88-04-001 or 90-11-063 appeared in the results); compilers.iecc.com is blocked by the egress proxy, so the page was never opened and the exact article could not be pinned, hence benchmark_url is null. Timings are from 1988 hardware and 1988 flex. The flex repository (README, NEWS, ONEWS, manual doc/flex.texi) contains no lex timings; its manual only says -f/-F is 'much faster (factor of 2-3)' than -C (flex against itself) and that -l compatibility costs performance. Search snippets also say re2c -b scanners are faster than flex -Cf ones. License text in COPYING is flex's own BSD-style wording (BSD-3-Clause-like, with a no-endorsement clause); the awesome-c list tags it BSD-2-Clause.
found_via: seed-record pass from the awesome-c Lexing and Parsing list entry given in the task lead; numbers surfaced by WebSearch 'flex vs AT&T lex scanner speed benchmark' and 'AT&T lex flex Sun 3/60 29.8 seconds 19.3 seconds 7.8 seconds scanner timings'
